notes.meaning: Elihu keeps speaking because he is not done explaining God's ways. He wants Job to see that there is still a good case to be made for the Almighty. This begins his final speech to help Job understand God's justice.

Elihu asks his listeners to be patient with him just a little longer. He insists that he still has important words to offer on God's behalf. He sees himself as an advocate defending God's honor and fairness.

Elihu says he will gather his arguments from far and wide, pointing to God's vast works in creation. His goal is to show that his Maker is completely fair and righteous in everything He does. We can trust that God never treats anyone unjustly.

Elihu promises that his words will be completely honest and free from lies. He describes himself as someone speaking with true, sincere knowledge rather than tricky arguments. He wants Job to listen with an open mind.

differ.view: The one who is perfect in knowledge refers to God Himself, who watches and weighs every human word and action.

notes.meaning: God possesses infinite strength, yet He never treats anyone with cold contempt. His great power is guided by perfect understanding, so He pays close attention to the needs of ordinary people. No person is too small for God to care about.

God does not guarantee a safe, thriving life for the wicked. Instead, He steps up to defend the poor and mistreated, giving them the justice they deserve. God makes sure that the cries of the hurting are answered.

God never looks away from righteous people, those who love and obey Him. He watches over them and can raise them up to places of great honor, seating them like kings on thrones. God never forgets those who belong to Him.

Sometimes good people find themselves trapped in pain or held down by troubles, as if locked in iron chains. These hardships are not meant to destroy them, but to correct them in love. God is still working for their good even in their lowest moments.

God uses hard times to show people where their lives have gone wrong. He reveals hidden faults and shows how pride has led them to step over the line into sin. Seeing our faults clearly helps us turn back to God with humble hearts.

God uses discipline to open their ears so they will finally pay attention. He gives a direct command for them to turn away from iniquity, which means doing what is wrong and sinful. Hard times can make us willing to listen to God.

If people listen to God's correction and serve Him faithfully, they will finish their lives in peace and happiness. Obedience to God brings deep inward joy and true blessing. Serving God with an honest heart brings the greatest contentment.

If people refuse to listen to God's correction, they bring about their own ruin. They will fall under judgment, perish by the sword, and die in foolish rebellion without true spiritual knowledge. Resisting God's guidance leads only to regret.

Ungodly people who are insincere in heart bottle up bitter anger against God. When He sends troubles to correct them, their pride keeps them from crying out to Him for help. Refusing to pray when life hurts only makes the burden heavier.

Those who stubbornly turn away from God often cut their lives short in their youth. Their lives end in shame among the corrupt and disgraceful. Living in rebellion against God wastes the precious gift of life.

God actually uses suffering as a tool to rescue the afflicted. By sending hardship, He opens their ears so they can hear what He has to say and be spared from deeper danger. Difficult moments can become the very medicine that heals our soul.

Elihu tells Job that God wanted to pull him out of tight distress into an open space of safety and peace. If Job had yielded to God's teaching, his table would now be loaded with rich, satisfying food. Submitting to God clears the path to blessing.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars translate this as describing Job's past life, arguing that God had previously brought Job into great freedom and wealth, which ended up making him careless.

notes.meaning: Elihu warns Job that he is currently acting just like the wicked by arguing against God's fairness. Because Job took the side of complaining rebels, divine justice has seized him like a prisoner. Murmuring against God puts a person on dangerous ground.

Job must be careful because God's anger against sin is real, and a sudden stroke of judgment could sweep him away. If God decides to strike, no mountain of money or huge ransom can buy a person's freedom. Earthly wealth cannot purchase a pardon from God.

Elihu asks if Job's wealth or mighty personal efforts can keep him out of trouble. No pile of gold or strong human force can stop God's hand when He acts. Only God has the power to truly deliver someone from distress.

Elihu warns Job not to long for the night of death, which Job had repeatedly begged for in his misery. Wanting to die can put a person straight into God's judgment rather than bringing true rest. We should leave the timing of death in God's hands.

Elihu urges Job to watch his spirit and not turn to sin by accusing God of being unfair. Job was choosing to vent his complaints rather than patiently bearing his trial. It is far worse to commit sin than to endure pain.

God shows His unmatched majesty through His mighty power, and no teacher can ever compare to Him. He uses His word and life's trials to instruct His people with perfect wisdom and patience. We should always approach God as humble learners.

No one has the right to give God instructions or tell Him how to run His universe. No human being can point an accusing finger at Him and say He has done wrong. God is completely free and perfectly fair in everything He does.

Elihu reminds Job to praise and lift up God's marvelous works rather than finding fault with them. Throughout history, people have celebrated God's power and governing care in songs of praise. Worship turns our focus away from our own complaints.

Everyone can look out and see the wonders God has made in creation. Even from a distance, human beings can look upon His greatness and see His hand at work. God's majesty is clear for anyone willing to notice.

God is far greater than human minds can ever fully grasp, and His eternal life cannot be measured in years. He has always existed and will never end, while humans understand only a small part of His ways. We must revere the God whose greatness has no limits.

God draws up tiny particles of water into the sky and gathers the vapor into rain clouds. He wisely arranges for water to fall in gentle drops rather than destructive torrents. His design in nature shows both His wisdom and His kindness.

The clouds pour down rain in rich supply to water the ground and help humanity. God sends these showers to refresh the fields and provide food for everyone. Creation faithfully reflects God's generous care for people.

No human can fully grasp how God spreads out the thick canopy of storm clouds across the sky. No one can explain how thunder crashes from the dark clouds, which serve like His royal tent. His mysterious works should quiet our proud opinions.

God scatters bright flashes of lightning across the cloudy canopy of heaven. The flash is so intense that it illuminates the stormy sky and pierces deep into the ocean waters. God rules over both the highest skies and the deepest seas.

God uses the clouds and storms for two very different tasks in His governing of the world. Through heavy floods and violent weather He brings judgment on nations, yet through gentle rain He provides plenty of food. God holds both justice and mercy in His hands.

God covers His hands with the fiery light of lightning and commands it to strike its exact target. He directs each flash like an archer hitting a mark, showing that nature is under His absolute command. Even the lightning obeys His orders without fail.

The roaring thunder announces that God is near and that a great storm is breaking. Even the farm animals sense the coming tempest and head for cover before the rain begins. Nature instinctively recognizes the power of the Creator.
